Question: What is the difference between the representation task and the learning-to-learn task?
Evidence:
[E1] (text, Section 6, page 8): We have collected a second dataset of photographs of spherical objects with complex appearance (glossy objects under natural light). In particular we use 3 different materials and 5 different illuminations each with 5 images from registered views (Fig. 11 ) for training and 70 for testing. Please see the supplemental video for the animation. Transfer of appearance captured from a real world image sequence to other complex geometry is shown in Fig. 12 . Tbl. 2 summarizes the outcome for the representation task previously explored for synthetic data only. An example result is seen in Fig. 1 , more are shown in the supplemental materials. Our method can estimate view-dependent appearance, unlike RM/RM++, from a small training set, but it
[E2] (text, Section 5.2, page 6): Tbl. 1 , top part, shows results as mean error across the data set. We see that for all data sets our method is a better representation in terms of having a lower DSSIM error. The difference in error is more pronounced for N OVEL V IEW than for S AME V IEW . A detailed plot of error distribution is seen in Fig. 6 , left. This is, as classic reﬂectance map captures appearance for a ﬁxed viewer location, for changing geometry, but does not generalize when the viewer moves. Arguably, classic RMs look qualitatively plausible without a reference, but only have low quantitative similarity (SSIM) in novel views.
[E3] (text, Section abstract, page 1): and-segmentation task, mapping from an image showing multiple materials to multiple deep appearance maps.
[E4] (figure, Figure 3, page 4) (image attached): Figure 3. Different appearance processing tasks that we address using our deep appearance maps. a) The ﬁrst task simply reproduces a given appearance, i. e., it maps from normal and view directions to RGB values using a NN. b) In a learning-to-learn task a network maps an image to a DAM representation. c) Finally, in the segmentation-and-estimation task, a network maps an image to multiple DAMs and multiple segmentation networks.
[E5] (figure, Figure 3, page 4): a zoomed view of Figure 3 (image attached)
[E6] (table, Table 1, page 7): Table 1. Quantitative results on synthetic data. Rows are different combination of tasks and methods (three applications, two view protocols, our two methods). Columns are different data. Error is measured as mean DSSIM across the data set (less is better).

  row 'Representation': 'View' = Same; 'Method' = RM++; 'Error' = .143; '' = .160
  row '(Sec. 3.2)': 'View' = ; 'Method' = OUR; 'Error' = .144; '' = .164
  row 'Learn-to-learn': 'View' = Same; 'Method' = SGD; 'Error' = .105; '' = .123
  row '(Sec. 3.3)': 'View' = ; 'Method' = OUR; 'Error' = .165; '' = .173
  row 'Segmentation': 'View' = Same; 'Method' = KMEANS; 'Error' = .132; '' = .136

These claims are already verified and kept:
- The representation task involves mapping from normal and view directions to RGB values using a neural network (NN), as shown in Figure 3a.
- The learning-to-learn task maps an image to a DAM representation, as depicted in Figure 3b.

These claims failed the checks; write corrected claims to replace them:
- "The representation task focuses on capturing appearance from a real-world image sequence, while the learning-to-learn task aims to generalize appearance across different geometries.": support check: The evidence in E1 (Section 6) discusses the transfer of appearance from a real-world image sequence to other complex geometries, but it does not provide a direct comparison between the representation and learning-to-learn tasks as described in the claim. The evidence in E4 (Figure 3) only describes the tasks but does not specify the focus or aim of each task as stated in the claim.
- "The representation task is characterized by a lower DSSIM error for the same view, as shown in Table 1.": E6 Method = OUR/View = Same is None, the claim says .144 [image]
